How I can help

Your stack will never match anyone's CV exactly, so I don't sell a particular technology; I sell a solved business problem. My core is production LLM systems. Around it I rely on a method rather than a claim: map the code first, pin down what it does today with tests, then change it, with every change checked by a reviewer that did not write it. That is how I added a security feature to a 20-year-old Rails application on a stack I had never used.

  • Build an AI product or feature

    From a business goal to a feature in production, with an evaluation baseline so you know it works before your users depend on it. Fixed scope, priced per deliverable.

    For founders and product teams

  • Make an LLM system reliable

    Your RAG or agent works in the demo and fails in production. I find out why and fix it. You get a ranked failure report and the fixes.

    For teams already shipping AI

  • Lead AI engineering in your team

    A lead or staff-level engineer inside your team on a long-term contract: architecture, delivery, a practical way to use AI in development, and direct work with product and leadership on what to build and why.

    For companies building an AI capability

  • Take over legacy code

    Old, critical code that nobody on the team wrote and nobody dares to touch. I map it, pin down what it does today with tests, then change it safely.

    For teams with code older than the team

How I work

  1. Start from the business number

    What is it worth if it works, and what does it cost when it fails? That decides the architecture and the budget, including where an LLM is the wrong tool.

  2. Build the evaluation first

    A test set and a scoring rubric come before the feature, so that "better" is a number rather than an opinion.

  3. Verify independently

    Generation is cheap; verification is the bottleneck. Every output passes checks that the agent which produced it does not control.

  4. Hand over something you own

    The code, the evaluation harness and the documentation stay with you, and so does the knowledge of how it works.

Selected work

Mobile-app company · 2025–2026

When hiring stopped adding output

The situation
The business grew by launching new apps, and the 12-person team I led had hit a ceiling: every new hire added coordination rather than output.
What I did
I built and ran an automated software factory: AI agents that design and code the apps, each output checked by an independent verifier, with a cost limit on every run.
The result
One engineer and one QA engineer outshipped the whole team.
Technical details

Multi-agent pipeline covering design, code, store assets and promo websites; model routing by task across Claude, Gemini and OpenAI; LLM-as-judge audits on a severity rubric. Architected its Google Cloud platform (Gemini and Claude on Vertex AI, Cloud Run, IAP, Secret Manager, Cloud Logging) and multimodal text-and-image search over the company's catalogue of 2,000+ apps. Replaced a paid low-code admin platform with an in-house dashboard. In my last week: 10 production apps in 3–4 days against the team's plateau of about 8 a week, at about $6 per app in model APIs.

Same company · 2020–2024

New distribution for a 200-app portfolio

The situation
I owned a portfolio of about 200 mobile apps end to end and worked with the business owners on budgets and ROI to keep it profitable.
What I did
On my own initiative I tested two additional app stores, brought the numbers to the business and, once it approved, ran the full launch.
The result
Two new distribution channels, released from the same codebase as everything else.
Technical details

Huawei AppGallery and Samsung Galaxy Store, next to Google Play, Amazon and Xiaomi: five stores from one Android codebase with per-store builds. A shared app template reused 80–90% of the code.

Enterprise and open source

Changing old, critical code safely

The situation
Large codebases that nobody on the current team wrote, running in production.
What I did
Four years of third-line support on enterprise systems, and recently a security feature in a 20-year-old Rails application on a stack I had never used.
The result
On the Rails application, existing behaviour was pinned by tests before the first change, and every change was checked by a reviewer that did not write it.
Technical details

2006–2010 at EPAM: on the maintenance team of a large Thomson Reuters programme I diagnosed production failures with the client's engineers, migrated a live database while changing its schema, and coordinated deployments. 2026: personal access tokens for Redmine 6.1.2 (Ruby on Rails), built with code maps, implementing subagents and a five-axis verification gate: 39 issues, 75 recorded attacks, 4,674 lines of tests, with the full process record published next to the code.

About

I'm a physicist by training. I started out writing C++ simulations for CERN's LHC experiments, then spent more than 20 years building software and leading engineering teams.

I founded a mobile games studio and grew it to a team of seven, negotiating partnerships with publishers and ad networks and running hiring, finances and KPIs. I was brought in as interim COO to stabilise a startup, analysing its profitability and guiding a pivot. For six years I was the lead engineer at a mobile-app company, working with the business owners on budgets and ROI and with the executive team on strategy. I have worked remotely since 2010.

In 2025 I rebuilt my own delivery around AI. The lesson I took from it: generation isn't the bottleneck, verification is.
